title: Chapter V
focus: horror at the moment of creation

teacherSummary.text: On a dreary November night, the creature opens its 'dull yellow eye.' Horrified by its appearance, Victor flees, dreams of Elizabeth turning into his mother's corpse, and wakes to see the creature reaching toward him. He runs into the street, meets Clerval, and collapses into a long fever, nursed by Henry.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Chapter V,” how does Shelley show horror at the moment of creation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter V, how does Shelley develop the idea of horror at the moment of creation? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter V develops the idea of horror at the moment of creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter V (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of horror at the moment of creation. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter V suggests about horror at the moment of creation. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's imagery and tone / mood), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses imagery in Chapter V to complicate the reader's understanding of horror at the moment of creation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter V within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of horror at the moment of creation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter V alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of horror at the moment of creation follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter V and its treatment of horror at the moment of creation. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's imagery and tone / mood, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter V as evidence for a larger claim about horror at the moment of creation in Frankenstein. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter V as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of horror at the moment of creation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Was the creature's first gesture threatening or loving? Use evidence. No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are agitates, palpitated, infusing, relapses, lassitude. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: ““Compose yourself,” said Clerval, who observed my change of colour, “I will not mention it, if it agitates you; but your father and cousin would be very happy if they received a letter from you in your own handwriting.” In this sentence it means: upsets; disturbs. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Gothic novels used darkness, storms and nightmares to produce dread. The quoted lines from Coleridge's 'Ancient Mariner' reinforce Victor's guilt. Why does this chapter matter? The irony is sharp: the being Victor labored to make is abandoned within minutes. The creature's outstretched hand may be a gesture of affection that Victor reads as threat. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for imagery.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “I continued walking in this manner for some time, endeavouring, by bodily exercise, to ease the load that weighed upon my mind.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to horror at the moment of creation? I circle “palpitated”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find imagery, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for imagery.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of imagery. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Imagery, Tone / mood, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how Chapter V develops the idea of horror at the moment of creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and tone / mood shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about horror at the moment of creation, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how imagery shapes horror at the moment of creation. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.

provenance: Original Liber et Libri pilot content; modern contextual vocabulary definitions (curated, based on Princeton WordNet 3.0); word histories only where verified (Online Etymology Dictionary); quotations from the public-domain text.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the chapter to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
